# Rung B (`rung-int-semantics-compiled`): the compiled path's integer rules of 2026-09-22

problem: on the compiled path `3 LSHIFT 32` on `ZZ32` answered 3, `|0|` and `-0` threw `IntegerOverflow`, `0 DOT 5` on `ZZ64` threw, `DOTMINUS 0` answered the maximum and `narrow` of an out-of-range `NN64` or `ZZ64` threw — explorations/compile-ladder/rung-int-semantics-compiled/probes/IntSemTable-compiled-before.txt:3
spec: for the guards and the multiplies, `|x|` is `x` unless it is negative (`Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:624-625`), unary `-` is the negative (`:384`), `DIV` truncates and throws only on a zero divisor (`:444-445`, `:459`), `·` is the product (`:415`), all carried to the fixed widths by `:75-77`, and an integer operation overflows only when its result is not representable; for `LSHIFT`, `RSHIFT` and `narrow` the prose is silent (`grep -rn 'LSHIFT\|RSHIFT\|narrow' Specification/basic Specification/basic-lib` prints nothing) and the rules built are Pavol's of 2026-09-22 — Specification/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:155
precedent: the team's own signed-count shift natives, which test a negative count first and saturate a far-negative one before any negation (`intShift`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:365-380`; `longShift`, `simpleLongArith.java:334-348`), with the interpreter's saturation at the width (`interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:173-183`); for the guards the in-file spelling of the minimum (`simpleIntArith.java:258`); for `narrow` the wrapping natives the prelude already imports — ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:51
deviation: the four new shift natives let bits fall where `intShift`/`longShift` throw on a lost bit, because the decided rule makes `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` bit operators — ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java:370
deviation: the `ZZ32` natives take an `int` count where the interpreter's take a `long`, because the compiled `LSHIFT` on `ZZ32` declares a `ZZ32` count — ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:259
deviation: `longOverflowingMul` and `longSaturatingMul` replace the team's guard-and-divide check with `Math.multiplyExact`, which also answers the minimum for a product equal to it, where the old check threw — ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleLongArith.java:70
deviation: `narrow` on `ZZ64` and `NN64` leaves the prelude convention rung W followed (a plainly named member takes the Overflowing native), which the getter `asZZ32` keeps — ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:581
deviation: against the specification's spelling, none: the prose names neither operator nor `narrow`, and its `shift` is not declared on this path (batch record, B, "No declaration goes into the compiler prelude") — Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:696
historical: ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleIntArith.java, ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleLongArith.java, ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:659

The `historical:` line names three files of the 2012 tree; the line number on its last entry is only there because the block's form asks every line to end in one. The other two edited files, `library_tests/IntConversionsRungW.fss` and `library_tests/IntegralOpsRungN.fss`, and the new test are the revival's own.

## 1. What the rung does

It builds, on the compiled path only, the four integer rules Pavol decided on 2026-09-22 (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:73-76`), with both of the coordinator's riders applied: siblings = with, signed narrow = truncates.

| rule | ledger row | edit |
|---|---|---|
| (a) `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` use the smart-shift rule | 335 (compiled half) | four new natives `intBitLeftShift`, `intBitRightShift` (`simpleIntArith.java:353-362`) and `longBitLeftShift`, `longBitRightShift` (`simpleLongArith.java:322-331`); imported at `CompilerBuiltin.fss:72-73` and `:198-199`; the four bodies at `CompilerBuiltin.fss:647-648` (`ZZ64`) and `:736-737` (`ZZ32`) call them. `<<`, `>>` and `<<<` are unchanged. |
| (c) the six zero guards test the minimum | 333 | `simpleIntArith.java:80`, `:85`, `:90`; `simpleLongArith.java:80`, `:85`, `:90` (`:89`, `:94`, `:99` before the edit) |
| siblings (rider "with") | new, provisional 378 | the ten guards in eight more methods of the same two files: `intSaturatingDiv`, `intSaturatingNeg`, `intSaturatingAbs` (`simpleIntArith.java:274`, `:279`, `:284`); `longSaturatingDiv`, `longSaturatingNeg`, `longSaturatingAbs` (`simpleLongArith.java:249`, `:254`, `:259`); `longOverflowingMul` and `longSaturatingMul` (two guards each) become `Math.multiplyExact` (`simpleLongArith.java:70-76`, `:239-245`) |
| (d) `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits | 346 (compiled half) | `ZZ64.narrow` → `jLongWrappingToInt` (`CompilerBuiltin.fss:659`); `NN64.narrow` → `jLongWrappingToUnsignedInt` (`:879`); `asZZ32` (`:581`) keeps its throw. Rung W's five throw assertions are reversed (`library_tests/IntConversionsRungW.fss:43-45`, `:63-64`) and its two `shouldOverflow` helpers, used by nothing else, are gone. |

The comment at `library_tests/IntegralOpsRungN.fss:187` now reads "For a count in 0..31, LSHIFT and RSHIFT agree with the << and >> of the same trait."; no assertion there changed.

Nothing is declared: `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` is untouched (its `LSHIFT`, `RSHIFT` and `narrow` declarations are at `:196-197`, `:206`, `:259-260`, `:386`). The four `import java` bindings are component-level imports in `CompilerBuiltin.fss`, of the kind the batch record's section B names as the natives' option ("bound in the import blocks at CompilerBuiltin.fss:25-74 and :155-196").

## 2. Where the fix belongs

The compiler prelude's integer types are flat traits each carrying its own operators (`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md`, §4.3, `ZZ32` at `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:201-255` before this rung and unchanged by it). Every answer this rung changes is computed by a prelude body over a Java native, so the fix is in the natives and the bodies, not in the checker or the code generator.

One earlier phase could answer these operators before the prelude does: `INTEGERLITERALFOLDING`, which runs before `TYPECHECK` (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:57`, `:142`). Its binary folder (`compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:58-108`) folds `+`, `-`, the multiplications, `DIV`, `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`, `CHOOSE` and the comparisons, and nothing else, so `LSHIFT`, `RSHIFT` and `narrow` of numerals still reach the prelude. Its unary folder (`:150-157`) answers `-`, `BOXMINUS`, `DOTMINUS` and `|…|` of a numeral exactly with `BigInteger`. So the zero-guard defect never showed on a numeral operand, only on a variable, which is why the test binds every operand to a typed variable.

## 3. Precedent search

- **Shifts: the team has written a shift count's range three ways.** (1) Masking: the eight `…ByIntMod32`/`…ByLongMod64` natives (`simpleIntArith.java:337-351`, `simpleLongArith.java:306-320`), which are Java's `<<`/`>>` and reduce the count modulo the width. (2) Signed counts with an overflow check: `intShift`, `longShift`, `unsignedIntShift`, `unsignedLongShift` (`simpleIntArith.java:365-380`, `simpleLongArith.java:334-348`, `simpleUnsignedIntArith.java:203-217`, `simpleUnsignedLongArith.java:207`), which test `b < 0` first, answer a count below `-31` (`-63`) with the sign before negating, and throw when a bit would be lost. (3) The interpreter's saturation at the width, `glue/prim/Int.java:173-183` and `Long.java:183-193`. The new natives take (2)'s handling of the negative count, including the far-negative test before `-b`, and (3)'s saturation at the width; they do not take (2)'s throw, which the decision of 2026-09-22 rejected. Rung N's bodies copied (1), which is how the compiled `LSHIFT` came to mask the count (row 335).
- **Guards: 16 sites.** `grep -rnE '([a-z]) ?== ?\(?-\1\b' ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/` finds exactly sixteen `x==(-x)` tests, all in the two edited files: the six of row 333 and the ten siblings (`simpleIntArith.java:274`, `:279`, `:284`; `simpleLongArith.java:71`, `:76`, `:249`, `:253`, `:265`, `:270`, `:275`, numbered before the edit). All sixteen are gone. The team's earlier repair of this defect (rung N guarding the divisor `-1` inside `REM`, `CompilerBuiltin.fss:601`, `:686`) worked around the guard at the caller. The spelling `Integer.MIN_VALUE`/`Long.MIN_VALUE` is already used in these files (`simpleIntArith.java:258`, `simpleLongArith.java:229`).

- **The product equal to the minimum.** `-2^32 · 2^31` is `-2^63`, which a `ZZ64` holds; `:415` makes it the answer, and the old check threw (below, §6).
- **Row 335, `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT`.** No prose chapter, and no api rendering, names either operator: `grep -rln 'LSHIFT\|RSHIFT' Specification Specification-1.0-frozen` prints nothing. The spec's arithmetic `shift` (`basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:696-702`) is a different operation, ⌊x·2^k⌋ on ℤ, and its prose is where "negative values of k shift the bits to the right" comes from. The rules built are Pavol's decision of 2026-09-22 (`POSITIONS.md:73`), which this rung executes and does not re-derive.
- **Row 346, `narrow`.** No prose chapter names `narrow` (same grep). The rule is Pavol's (`POSITIONS.md:76`), with the coordinator's rider "signed narrow = truncates".

## 5. Decisions taken inside the rung

1. **The shift rule lives in four new natives, not in Fortress bodies over `<<` and `>>`.** The alternative was a four-branch body per operator (`if other >= 32 then 0 elif other >= 0 then self << other elif other <= -32 then self >> 31 else self >> (-other) end`), with no Java change. The natives were chosen because the team's precedent for signed shift counts is a native (`intShift`), because one native call is the machine shift the decision asks for, and because a body would add three compiled comparisons and a negation to every shift.
2. **Names: `intBitLeftShift`, `intBitRightShift`, `longBitLeftShift`, `longBitRightShift`.** They sit with `intBitNot`/`intBitAnd`/… because the decision calls these "bit operators". The word "Saturating" was not used because in these two files it means clamping to the type's maximum or minimum (`intSaturatingAdd`), which is a different thing from a shift saturating to 0 or -1. The alternative that follows the neighbouring names, `…ByIntMod32`, would have been `…ByIntSaturating32`.
3. **`Math.multiplyExact` rather than the minimum test plus a zero line.** The brief offered both. The minimum test plus a zero line would have been the smaller edit to the team's shape, but that shape has a second defect: its check `Long.MAX_VALUE / |a| < |b|` is false only when `|a|·|b| ≤ 2^63-1`, so it throws for a product equal to `-2^63`. The before-capture shows it: `ZZ64 -2^32 2^31 = IntegerOverflow` (`probes/IntSemTable-compiled-before.txt:52`). `Math.multiplyExact` is Java 8, the JVM's own exact check, and has neither defect; the saturating twin catches its `ArithmeticException` and returns the sign-correct limit with the file's own formula (`((a^b) >> 63) ^ Long.MAX_VALUE`, `simpleLongArith.java:244`, unchanged from the old `:259`). The `int` multiplies are not touched: they widen to `long` and have no guard.
4. **The four saturating natives that no prelude body uses are tested by importing them into the test**, following `IntegerChoose1.fss:13`. The alternative was to change them without an assertion, since no Fortress program can reach them through an operator.
5. **Signed `narrow` truncates.** The tail carries two sentences about this rider; the rider's value set at launch is "truncates", so `ZZ64.narrow` truncates and all five of rung W's assertions are reversed. The sentence beginning "With signed narrow = unchanged" is the conditional for the other value and was not applied.
6. **`2^31` as a `ZZ64` is computed as `2^32 DIV 2` in the test**, not written as the numeral `2147483648`, whose bit length is 32 (FACTS, the literal-wrap lines).
7. **The interpreter's silent wrap: a ledger row, and no expected-failure test in this rung.** See §9, row 379.

decisions: The shift rule is in four new natives (intBitLeftShift/intBitRightShift, longBitLeftShift/longBitRightShift), not in Fortress bodies over << and >>. The rejected alternative was a four-branch body per operator ('if other >= 32 then 0 elif other >= 0 then self << other elif other <= -32 then self >> 31 else self >> (-other) end'), which needs no Java. Natives were chosen for three reasons: the team's precedent for signed counts is a native (intShift), one native call is the machine shift the decision asks for, and a body adds three compiled comparisons and a negation to every shift.

The natives are named in the Bit family (they sit beside intBitNot/intBitAnd, and the decision calls them 'bit operators'). The rejected alternative was '...ByIntSaturating32' after the neighbouring '...ByIntMod32'. In these files 'Saturating' means clamping to MAX/MIN (intSaturatingAdd), which is a different thing from a shift saturating to 0 or -1.

Math.multiplyExact replaces the guard-and-divide check in longOverflowingMul and longSaturatingMul. The rejected alternative, which the brief also offered, was testing Long.MIN_VALUE plus a zero line. That keeps a second defect: Long.MAX_VALUE/|a| < |b| rejects a product equal to -2^63 (measured: -2^32 * 2^31 threw, probes/IntSemTable-compiled-before.txt:52). multiplyExact is Java 8 and the JVM's own check. The saturating twin catches its ArithmeticException and returns the file's existing sign formula ((a^b) >> 63) ^ Long.MAX_VALUE. The int multiplies widen to long and have no guard, so they were not touched.

The four saturating natives that no prelude body calls (intSaturatingDiv/Abs, longSaturatingDiv/Abs) are asserted by importing them into the test, as library_tests/IntegerChoose1.fss:13 does. The rejected alternative was to fix them with no assertion, since no operator reaches them.
